topic.title: Planning an investigation: variables, hypotheses, risk, apparatus, tables and diagrams
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Unit 7 is a quarter of the award: Booklet A is three one-hour practical tasks done in school (15 marks each), and Booklet B is three 30-minute written papers (35 marks each) sat in the Summer, every question set in a practical. Planning is asked on every Booklet B paper: variables, instruments, precautions and table headings for a mark each, a labelled apparatus diagram for three or four, and a six-mark method written in full sentences.
mustMemorise: Independent variable: the one you change; dependent: the one you measure; controlled: kept the same
A hypothesis predicts a direction linking the two variables and gives a scientific reason
Valid: only the independent variable changes. Reliable: repeats agree. Accurate: close to the true value
Weight = mass × g (g = 10 N/kg); work done = force × distance; power = work done ÷ time, in watts
Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot, in N m or N cm
In equilibrium, the clockwise moments about a pivot equal the anticlockwise moments
Estimate = mean per quadrat × area of the habitat ÷ area of one quadrat
Table headings are quantity / unit; the independent variable goes in the first column
Apparatus diagrams: two-dimensional, assembled, open paths, every piece labelled
notOnThisSpec: Uncertainty, percentage error and statistical tests of data
Systematic and random error named as such: CCEA asks about accuracy, reliability and validity
Risk scored on a scale (likelihood times severity): the specification asks for hazard, risk and control

mustKnow: weight = mass × g, with g = 10 N/kg
work done = force × distance moved along the line of the force
moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot
clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments about a pivot, for a body in equilibrium

notOnThisSpec: Uncertainty, percentage error and statistical tests
Risk scored on a numerical scale

mustBeAbleTo: Name the independent, dependent and controlled variables in the experiment's own terms
Write a testable hypothesis: a direction linking the two variables and a scientific reason
Write a method in numbered steps with the apparatus, the amounts, the readings and the repeat
Choose the instrument for each reading, and find the volume of an irregular solid by displacement
Pair each hazard with a specific control and a reason tied to it
Set out a results table with the independent variable first and quantity / unit headings
Draw apparatus as an assembled two-dimensional cross-section with open paths and labels
Tell valid, reliable and accurate apart, and say what improves each
Find personal power from weight, vertical height and time
Use the Principle of Moments to find an unknown weight or distance
Estimate a population from quadrat counts: mean × area of the habitat ÷ area of one quadrat
Tell a control, an extra test without the working factor, from a controlled variable, and set one up with the volume matched
sheet.howExamined: Booklet A is three practical tasks done in school, one each for Biology, Chemistry and Physics, 15 marks each: you record your own readings to the stated precision, process them and answer questions on the variables, the method and the result. Booklet B is three 30-minute written papers of 35 marks, sat in the Summer at the same tier: every question is set in a practical, one question in each is a six-mark method marked in bands on the number of points and the quality of your writing, and the rest are one- and two-mark parts: name the instrument, identify a variable, give a precaution and its reason, head a table, label or draw apparatus. The Summer 2019, 2025 and 2026 Booklet B papers each set a planning method as the six-mark question.
traps: Measuring an irregular solid with a ruler, or multiplying mass by volume, instead of displacement and density = mass ÷ volume (Summer 2025 Booklet B Physics Higher Q1)
Giving 'to improve accuracy' as the reason for a precaution or a repeat, where the scheme wants reliability (Summer 2025 Booklet B Physics Higher Q1 and Q2)
Leaving out the key that identifies the plants, or not naming the quadrat, in a sampling method (Summer 2025 Booklet B Biology Higher Q1 and Foundation Q3)
Two different diagrams, sealed-off funnels, blocked tubes or missing labels in an apparatus drawing (Summer 2024 Booklet B Chemistry Higher Q2; Summer 2025 Booklet B Chemistry Higher Q2)
Naming a variable loosely: the dependent variable had to be the compressed length, not just the length (Summer 2024 Booklet B Physics Higher Q4)
Giving the length of the wire, the variable being changed, as the controlled variable (Summer 2025 Booklet B Physics Foundation Q2)
Dividing the distance by the weight to find a moment, instead of multiplying (Summer 2024 Booklet A Physics Foundation and Higher Q1)
Stating the Principle of Moments without 'about a point' or 'in equilibrium', or subtracting forces that turn the same way (Summer 2025 Booklet B Physics Higher Q4)
Naming the quantity to be measured when the question asks for the instrument (Summer 2023 Booklet B Physics Foundation Q2)
Vague risk actions such as 'tell someone' or 'keep away from it', which name no control (Summer 2023 Booklet A Biology Foundation Q1)
A 'plastic screen' is not enough for a reactive metal in water: the control is a safety screen that shields you, with small pieces (Summer 2025 Booklet B Chemistry Foundation Q1)
General safety advice where a toxic gas needs a fume cupboard (Summer 2025 Booklet B Chemistry Foundation Q3)
An average typed as A + B ÷ 2 without brackets, giving a value outside the two readings (Summer 2024 Booklet A Biology Foundation Q1)
A scale-up made far more complicated than mean × area of the habitat ÷ area of one quadrat (Summer 2023 Booklet B Biology Foundation Q3)
The reason for standing both solutions in the bath before mixing: so the enzyme and substrate reach the reaction temperature, which most saw (Summer 2024 Booklet A Biology Higher Q1)

A student of weight 540 N runs up a flight of 18 identical steps in one fifth of a minute. Each step has a vertical rise of 0.16 m and a tread (depth) of 0.28 m.
Work out the work she does, then use it to calculate her power. Include the unit. [8]

steps.decision: Work against her weight depends only on how high she rises, so use the rise of each step, never the tread.

options: Her weight acts straight down, so only the vertical distance she moves counts
The tread is shorter, so it gives a smaller answer
The rise is the only length printed in metres
whyMenu.explain: Work done = force × the distance moved along the line of the force. Her weight is vertical, so the distance is the vertical height: the rises add up, and the treads play no part.

steps.working: Time = one fifth of 60 s = 12 s
steps.decision: Power is in watts, joules per second, so the time must be in seconds.
The equation first, then the numbers, then the value: each line earns its own mark.
Divide the work by the time in seconds.
The unit earns its own mark: watts, W.

workedExamples.stem:
A uniform metre rule rests on a pivot at its 30 cm mark. It balances when a 0.9 N weight hangs from its 5 cm mark. The rule's own weight W acts at its 50 cm mark.
Use the Principle of Moments to find W. Work in metres. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. [5]

steps.working: Distance of the 0.9 N weight from the pivot = 30 − 5 = 25 cm = 0.25 m
steps.decision: A moment uses the distance from the pivot, not the mark on the rule.
Moment = force × distance from the pivot: multiply, never divide.

steps.working: W acts at the 50 cm mark: 50 − 30 = 20 cm = 0.20 m from the pivot
steps.decision: A uniform rule's weight acts at its centre, its centre of gravity.

options: The rule is uniform, so its weight acts at its centre of gravity, the middle
Weight always acts at the end of an object
whyMenu.explain: The centre of gravity is the point where the whole weight can be taken to act. A uniform rule's is at its middle, the 50 cm mark, whatever the pivot's position.

steps.working: Clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment: W × 0.20 = 0.225, so W = 0.225 ÷ 0.20 = 1.125 N
steps.decision: The rule balances, so the principle holds; rearrange for W.
The question asks for 1 decimal place: that is a mark of its own.

workedExamples.stem:
A student places ten 0.5 m × 0.5 m quadrats at random in a meadow of area 450 m² and counts the dandelions in each: 3, 5, 2, 4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 2, 6.
Estimate the number of dandelions in the meadow. [4]

steps.decision: Add every count before you average.
The mean per quadrat evens out the random differences between quadrats.
A half-metre square covers a quarter of a square metre.

options: The mean is per quadrat, and a quadrat is not 1 m², so its area is needed to scale up
The area is needed to find the mean
whyMenu.explain: The mean counts dandelions in one quadrat. The meadow holds meadow area ÷ quadrat area quadrats' worth of ground, so the quadrat's own area decides the scale-up.

steps.decision: Mean per quadrat × area of the meadow ÷ area of one quadrat.

twin.stem: Eight 1 m² quadrats are placed at random on a lawn of area 90 m². The daisy counts are 7, 9, 6, 8, 10, 7, 9, 8. Estimate the number of daisies on the lawn.

items.stem: Before we start: what is the mean of 12 s, 15 s and 18 s?

options.feedback: Add the three, 45 s, and divide by how many there are, 3.
That is the total. A mean divides the total by the number of readings.
That divides only the last reading by 3. Put the sum in brackets: (12 + 15 + 18) ÷ 3.

items.stem: Which of these is a unit of force?

options.feedback: Force, weight included, is measured in newtons.
The kilogram is the unit of mass. On Earth, every kilogram weighs 10 N.
The joule is the unit of energy and of work done.

items.stem: Which piece of glassware measures 25 cm³ of a liquid most precisely?

options.feedback: It has a scale marked along its length, read at the bottom of the meniscus.
A beaker's marks are only a rough guide; it is for holding and mixing.
A conical flask is for holding a reaction mixture, not for measuring.
There are 1000 mm in a metre, so divide by 1000.
That divides by 100, which changes centimetres to metres, not millimetres.
That divides by 10. A metre is 1000 millimetres.

items.stem: A student investigates how the mass of a trolley affects the time it takes to roll down a ramp. What is the independent variable?

options.feedback: It is the variable the student changes on purpose.

options.text: the time to roll down the ramp
options.feedback: That is measured to see the effect: the dependent variable.
It stays the same for every run, so it is a controlled variable.

items.stem: A student repeats each measurement three times and takes the mean. What does this improve?

options.feedback: Repeats that agree can be trusted: that is reliability.
A faulty instrument gives the same error every time, so repeating cannot make a reading more accurate.

options.text: how close each reading is to the true value
options.feedback: Closeness to the true value is accuracy, which comes from the instrument and the technique, not from repeats.

items.stem: A solid heated in a crucible may spit out hot pieces. Which control belongs in the risk assessment?

options.feedback: It matches the hazard: hot pieces could reach the eyes.

options.text: tell the teacher before you start
options.feedback: It names no control, so it earns nothing.
Too vague to be a control; you still have to heat the crucible.

items.stem: What is a unit for a moment?

options.feedback: Newton metres, force times distance, or N cm when distances are in centimetres.
A moment is force multiplied by distance, so its unit is newtons times metres, not newtons per metre.
That is newtons per centimetre, a unit for a spring constant, not a moment.

items.stem: A drawing of apparatus shows a line across the end of a delivery tube. Why does it lose the mark?

options.text: The gas could not pass along the tube
options.feedback: Examiners treat a line across a tube as a blockage: the apparatus would not work.

options.text: The tube should have been drawn in three dimensions
options.feedback: Diagrams are two-dimensional cross-sections; drawing in 3-D loses marks.

options.text: The tube should not be labelled
options.feedback: Every piece should be labelled; the fault is the blocked end.

items.stem: How should a student find the volume of an irregular pebble?

options.text: lower it into water in a measuring cylinder and read the rise in level
options.feedback: Displacement: the pebble pushes aside its own volume of water.

options.text: measure its length, width and height with a ruler
options.feedback: An irregular shape has no single length, width or height to measure.
A balance gives its mass, not its volume.

items.stem: Which apparatus marks out the area in which plants are counted?

options.feedback: A square frame of known area, placed on the ground.
A quadrant is a quarter of a circle. The frame is a quadrat.

options.text: a patch chosen where the plants grow most thickly
options.feedback: Choosing where to look makes the sample unfair; quadrats go at random coordinates.

context.setting: A student plans to react magnesium ribbon with acid in a polystyrene cup

parts.stem: A student plans to react magnesium ribbon with hydrochloric acid. What should she use to measure the mass of the magnesium ribbon?

options.feedback: A balance measures mass, here to 0.01 g.
A measuring cylinder measures the volume of a liquid.
A thermometer measures temperature.
A stopwatch measures time.

parts.workedSolution: a balance. A balance measures mass, here to 0.01 g.

parts.stem: What should she use to measure 20 cm³ of the acid?

options.feedback: Read at eye level, at the bottom of the meniscus.
A beaker's marks are only rough; it holds liquids but does not measure them precisely.
A balance measures mass, not volume.
A thermometer measures temperature.

parts.workedSolution: a measuring cylinder. Read at eye level, at the bottom of the meniscus.

parts.stem: What should she use to measure the time for the magnesium to disappear?

options.feedback: Start it as the magnesium goes in and stop it when the last piece disappears.
A thermometer measures temperature, not time.
A metre rule measures length.
A balance measures mass.

parts.workedSolution: a stopwatch. Start it as the magnesium goes in and stop it when the last piece disappears.

context.setting: A bubble potometer beside a fan set to three speeds

parts.stem: A student uses a bubble potometer to find how the speed of a fan blowing on a leafy shoot affects how far the air bubble moves in 10 minutes. Identify the independent variable.

options.feedback: The student sets the fan to different speeds on purpose.

options.text: the distance the bubble moves in 10 minutes
options.feedback: That is measured to see the effect: the dependent variable.
It is kept the same: a controlled variable.

parts.workedSolution: the speed of the fan. The student sets the fan to different speeds on purpose.

parts.stem: Identify the dependent variable in the same investigation.

options.text: the distance the bubble moves in 10 minutes
options.feedback: It is what is measured each time, at each fan speed.
The fan speed is changed on purpose: the independent variable.
The same shoot is used throughout: a controlled variable.

scheme.for: the distance the bubble moves in 10 minutes

parts.workedSolution: the distance the bubble moves in 10 minutes. It is what is measured each time, at each fan speed.

parts.stem: Identify a variable the student must control.

options.feedback: Temperature also changes transpiration, so it must stay the same.
The fan speed is what is being tested, so it is changed, not controlled.
That is the result being measured, not a control.

parts.workedSolution: the temperature of the room. Temperature also changes transpiration, so it must stay the same.

context.setting: A results table for gas collected every 10 seconds

parts.stem: A student records the volume of gas collected in a gas syringe every 10 seconds. Which heading should the volume column have?

options.feedback: Quantity / unit, so every cell below holds a number only.
The unit is missing, the mark most often lost on tables and axes.
A unit alone does not say what was measured.

parts.workedSolution: Volume of gas / cm³. Quantity / unit, so every cell below holds a number only.

parts.stem: Which quantity goes in the first column of her table?

options.feedback: The time is the variable she chooses, every 10 seconds, so it comes first.
The volume is what she measures: it follows the time.
The mass is kept the same, so it needs no column of its own.

parts.workedSolution: Time / s. The time is the variable she chooses, every 10 seconds, so it comes first.

context.setting: Dilute sulfuric acid poured into a polystyrene cup

hints: Name something she wears, then say what it protects from the acid.

commonErrors.feedback: "Be careful" or "tell someone" names no control. Name what she wears, such as eye protection, and what it protects.

parts.stem:
Dilute sulfuric acid is an irritant. A student pours it into a polystyrene cup of sodium hydroxide solution, and it may splash.
Give one precaution she should take, and explain how it reduces the risk.

accepted: Wear eye protection, so that splashes of the acid cannot reach her eyes

scheme.for: a precaution against splashes: wear eye protection / goggles / safety glasses (or gloves)
a reason tied to that precaution: stops the acid reaching the eyes (or the skin)
scheme.examinerNote: The reason earns its mark only beside a right precaution.

parts.workedSolution: Wear eye protection (goggles), so that splashes of the irritant acid cannot reach her eyes.

context.setting: A student about to measure her personal power stands on bathroom scales

hints: Weight = mass × g, and g is 10 N/kg.
parts.stem:
Before measuring her personal power, a student stands on bathroom scales, which read 66 kg.
Calculate her weight, and give its unit. (g = 10 N/kg)

scheme.examinerNote: The unit mark stands on its own.

parts.workedSolution: weight = mass × g = 66 × 10 = 660 N

context.setting: Step-ups onto a gym box

parts.stem:
A student of mass 48 kg measures her personal power by stepping onto a gym box 350 mm high, 24 times, in 36 s.
Calculate her weight. Include the unit. (g = 10 N/kg)
parts.workedSolution: weight = 48 × 10 = 480 N

parts.stem: Write the height of the box, 350 mm, in metres.

commonErrors.feedback: 8400 is the distance in millimetres. Change 350 mm to 0.35 m first, then multiply by 24.

parts.stem: Calculate the total vertical distance through which she lifts her weight in the 24 step-ups, in metres.

commonErrors.feedback: 4032 J is the work done. Power is the rate of doing work: divide by the 36 s.

parts.stem: Work out the work she does, then her power. Include the unit.

context.setting: Thistles in a grazing field

hints: How many quadrats would it take to cover the whole field? Each one here covers more than 1 m².

commonErrors.feedback: 4320 would be right for 1 m² quadrats. These cover 4 m² each, so divide by 4 as well.

parts.stem:
Large quadrats measuring 2 m × 2 m are placed at random in a field 60 m long and 45 m wide. The mean number of thistles per quadrat is 1.6.
Use this to estimate the number of thistles in the field.

scheme.for: area of the field = 60 × 45 = 2700 m²; area of a quadrat = 4 m²

parts.workedSolution: Area of the field = 60 × 45 = 2700 m². Area of one quadrat = 2 × 2 = 4 m². Estimate = 1.6 × 2700 ÷ 4 = 1080

context.setting: A metre rule balanced at its centre with two weights

commonErrors.feedback: That divides the distance by the force. A moment is force × distance: 4.5 × 0.12.

parts.stem:
A metre rule is balanced at its centre. A 4.5 N weight hangs 0.12 m to the left of the pivot.
Calculate the moment of this weight about the pivot, in N m.

scheme.for: moment = force × distance from the pivot

parts.workedSolution: moment = force × distance = 4.5 × 0.12 = 0.54 N m

parts.stem: How far to the right of the pivot must a 2.7 N weight hang to balance the rule? Give your answer in m.
parts.workedSolution: Clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment: 2.7 × d = 0.54, so d = 0.54 ÷ 2.7 = 0.2 m

context.setting: Protease clearing milk at 15 °C, 25 °C and 35 °C

parts.stem: A student times how long protease takes to clear milk at 15 °C, 25 °C and 35 °C. Which is a testable hypothesis?

options.text: The higher the temperature, up to 35 °C, the shorter the time for the milk to clear
options.feedback: It links the two variables in a stated direction, so the results can show it right or wrong.
No direction is given, so no result could prove it wrong.
It does not mention the independent variable at all.

scheme.for: The higher the temperature, up to 35 °C, the shorter the time for the milk to clear

parts.workedSolution: The higher the temperature, up to 35 °C, the shorter the time for the milk to clear. It links the two variables in a stated direction, so the results can show it right or wrong.

hints: Start with what heating does to the molecules, then say what that means for the enzyme and the protein.

commonErrors.feedback: Enzymes are molecules, not living things, so they cannot be killed. Well below the optimum they simply work more slowly; above it they denature.

parts.stem: Explain, in terms of molecules, why the milk clears faster at 35 °C than at 15 °C.

accepted: At a higher temperature the molecules have more kinetic energy, so they collide more often and more enzyme-substrate complexes form

scheme.for: the molecules have more kinetic energy / move faster
more (successful) collisions / more enzyme–substrate complexes (in a given time)

context.setting: Estimating the dandelions on a school playing field

hints: Tell it in order: where the quadrats go, what happens in each one, then the calculation.

commonErrors.feedback: The frame is a quadrat; a quadrant is a quarter of a circle. Examiners also look for the key used to identify the plants.

parts.stem:
A student wants to estimate how many dandelions grow on a school playing field.
Describe how she should use quadrats to make the estimate, from placing them to the final calculation.
Your written communication is marked here too: answer in full sentences, in a sensible order, using the correct scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: At least five of the indicative points, in detail and in a sensible order; specialist terms used accurately; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is always clear. Sentences begin with capital letters and end with full stops.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist terms; spelling, punctuation and grammar clear enough for the meaning to be followed.
One or two of the indicative points; few specialist terms; the meaning may be unclear in places.

indicativeContent.point: lay two tape measures at right angles along two edges of the field
choose random numbers as coordinates for each quadrat
place a quadrat at each pair of coordinates
use a key to identify the dandelions
count the dandelions in each quadrat and record the counts
use many quadrats, for example ten or more
work out the mean number of dandelions per quadrat
scale up: mean × area of the field ÷ area of one quadrat

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place the answer within its band on the quality of the writing. Band A [5]–[6] at least five points; band B [3]–[4] three or four; band C [1]–[2] one or two; [0] nothing worthy of credit.
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. The quality of the writing decides the mark within the band, never the band itself.

parts.workedSolution: First she lays two tape measures at right angles along two edges of the field to make a pair of axes. She uses random numbers to choose coordinates, so that the quadrats are placed at random, and puts a quadrat at each pair of coordinates. In each quadrat she uses a key to identify the dandelions and counts them, recording each count in a table. She repeats this for at least ten quadrats. She works out the mean number of dandelions per quadrat. Finally she scales up: the estimate is the mean multiplied by the area of the field and divided by the area of one quadrat.

findTheMistake.stem:
Orla is asked: 'A 3.0 N weight hangs 28 cm from the pivot of a balanced metre rule. Calculate its moment about the pivot. [2]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: Moment = force × distance from the pivot
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is right: moment = force × distance. Line 2 then divides the distance by the force instead of multiplying them, so the moment comes out far too small. It should be 3.0 × 28 = 84 N cm.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of two: the equation in line 1 stands, and the value is lost with the division. Summer 2024 Booklet A examiners saw the distance divided instead of multiplied.

findTheMistake.stem:
Kai is asked: 'A pebble of mass 58.5 g is lowered into a measuring cylinder and the water level rises from 20.0 cm³ to 42.5 cm³. Calculate its density. [3]'
His answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The volume by displacement in line 2 is right. Line 3 multiplies the mass by the volume, but density = mass ÷ volume: 58.5 ÷ 22.5 = 2.6 g/cm³. A pebble a thousand times denser than water should have looked wrong.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of three: the volume stands; the equation and the value are lost. Summer 2025 Booklet B examiners found a significant minority multiplying the volume and the mass.

findTheMistake.stem:
Beth is asked: '8 quadrats, each 0.5 m × 0.5 m, placed at random in a field of area 280 m² hold 44 clover plants in all. Estimate the number of clover plants in the field. [3]'
Her answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are right, but line 3 never uses the quadrat's area: it treats each quadrat as 1 m². The field holds 280 ÷ 0.25 = 1120 quadrats' worth of ground, so the estimate is 5.5 × 280 ÷ 0.25 = 6160.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of three: the mean stands; the scale-up and its value are lost. Summer 2023 Booklet B examiners saw this calculation made harder than it is.

prompts.prompt: What must an apparatus diagram be to earn its marks?

findings.asked: Draw the apparatus for a distillation, name the round-bottom flask and condenser, explain the water flow and the thermometer position.
findings.wentWrong: Diagrams were very poor: two different diagrams offered, sealed-off funnels, apparatus that could not work, no labels; the flask and condenser were unfamiliar and the reasons for the water flow and thermometer position were rarely right - the practical had clearly not been seen.
findings.rule: Know the standard apparatus by name and by drawing before the exam; a diagram must work.

findings.asked: Draw the assembled apparatus for collecting gas from marble chips and acid.
findings.wentWrong: Generally good, but examiners want a two-dimensional cross-section with a clear path for gas: a line drawn across the end of a tube or a stopper counts as a blockage, and each piece must be recognisable.
findings.rule: 2-D, open paths, every piece recognisable and labelled.

findings.asked: Identify the variables in a spring investigation, then use F = ke.
findings.wentWrong: Variables were mostly right, but the dependent variable had to be the compressed length specifically; the unit of the spring constant was not well known.
findings.rule: Name the variable exactly as it is measured in this experiment; k is in N/m (or N/cm).

findings.asked: Plan how to find the density of an irregular solid, give a precaution and its reason, state the density equation.
findings.wentWrong: Many measured 'length, breadth and height' with a ruler, missing the word irregular; precautions were fine but 'to improve accuracy' was the common wrong reason; a significant minority wrote density = mass x volume.
findings.rule: Irregular solid: mass on a balance, volume by displacement; density = mass / volume.

findings.asked: Six-mark QWC on estimating plant abundance in a habitat.
findings.wentWrong: Most answers reached four marks or more, yet few mentioned a key for naming the species, and some could not name the quadrat.
findings.rule: Quadrat, random placement, key to identify, count, repeat and average, scale up.

findings.asked: Safety precautions when reacting sodium with water.
findings.wentWrong: Generally known; a 'glass screen' was not credited in place of a safety screen.
findings.rule: Safety = the specific hazard and the specific named control.

insight.ruleToRemember: A plan names the independent, dependent and control variables in the experiment's own terms, chooses apparatus by name, draws it as a labelled 2-D cross-section with open paths, states a specific hazard and control, and says what will be measured, how, and how many times. Repeating improves reliability, not accuracy.
insight.aStarSignal: A plan that a stranger could follow: named apparatus, a working diagram, exact variables, a results table with units, and a precaution with its reason.
